title: Flat-panel TV: safe teardown
summary: Get the LED backlight strips, diffuser and prism sheets, reflector, power board, speakers and main board out of an LCD or LED flat-panel TV. The power board's big capacitor can hold a dangerous charge after unplugging: measure and discharge it first. Large sets are heavy, the panel glass cuts, and older sets have mercury tubes.

steps.text: Unplug the TV and keep the plug where you can see it, or tape over its pins, so nobody plugs it back in while it is open. Pull out every other cable. Leave it at least 5 minutes.
Lay a thick blanket on the floor, or on a sturdy table bigger than the screen for a small set. Lay the TV face down on it and unscrew the stand.
steps.warn: Large sets are heavy: a 47-inch LCD can weigh about 40 kg. Sony says larger sets need two or more people. Unplug every cable first, hold the frame, never the screen, and don't lift a big set onto a table.

steps.text: Undo the screws around the back cover (often 10 to 20; some hide under the stand) and lift the cover straight up. Bag the screws.

Find the power board: the board the mains cord goes into, with the biggest round capacitors. First prove your meter works on a battery. Set it to DC volts (a meter rated 600 V or more), hold the probes behind their finger guards and use one hand only. Measure across the legs of the biggest capacitor, then across any other large capacitors and the backlight output connector pins. Discharge each with a resistor tool (2 to 5 kilohm, 10 W or more, held on for 10 seconds), then measure again. Every one must read under 1 V before you go on. Clip a wire across the big capacitor's legs and leave it there (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
steps.warn: These capacitors can hold about 170 V on 120 V mains, about 325 V on 230 V mains, or about 390 V on sets that boost the mains, for minutes after unplugging. The backlight driver, often on this board, can run LED strings at up to about 120 V. One hand only. Never short a capacitor with a screwdriver.

steps.text: Photograph every connector. Unplug the speaker leads, the backlight lead and the wide flat ribbon cable to the panel. On ribbon connectors, flip up the small locking bar first, then pull the cable straight out.

Unscrew and lift out the speakers, the power board, the main board and any small button or infrared board. Keep each board whole with its own screws. Older sets may have a separate inverter board for the backlight tubes: take it out the same way.
steps.warn: A CCFL inverter makes about 650 V AC while running. Unplugged, it holds only what its capacitors hold: measure and discharge them like the power board's.

steps.text: Undo the screws and clips around the front bezel or frame. With a helper on any set over about 32 inches, hold the frame, never the glass, and turn the set over so the screen faces up, then lift the bezel clear. Fold the small boards on the panel edge over onto the back of the panel and tape them there.
steps.warn: The thin flex strips joining these boards to the glass tear easily. Don't bend them sharply.

steps.text: With the screen facing up, lift the LCD panel out evenly by both long edges (two people for a big panel). Lay it flat on a large sheet of cardboard, well away from where you are working.
steps.warn: The panel is thin glass. It cracks if bent or pressed in the middle, and broken edges cut deep. Wear gloves and eye protection.

steps.text: Lift out the thin optical sheets one at a time from one corner, noting their order. Number each with a marker on its edge. Stack them flat between sheets of card.

Lift out the thick milky diffuser plate (or a clear plastic plate on edge-lit sets). Look behind the plate. If thin glass tubes lie on the reflector, this is an older CCFL set: go to the next step and leave the reflector alone until the tubes are out. If you see only LED strips, free the white reflector sheet from its tabs and lift it out, then skip the next step.

Older sets with CCFL tubes: unclip the lamp holders, unplug each thin glass tube and lift it out whole by its ends. Wrap each in paper. Leave them in place if you can't do this gently. Once the tubes are out, free the reflector sheet from its tabs and lift it out.
steps.warn: CCFL tubes hold mercury. If one breaks, everyone leaves the room with a window open for at least 15 minutes. Then, in gloves, pick up pieces with stiff card and tape, wipe with a damp cloth, seal it all in a glass jar and keep it outdoors. Don't vacuum.

steps.text: LED sets: unplug the strip leads. Strips are held by double-sided tape, clips or small screws. Undo screws or clips, or slide a thin flat tool under one end of a taped strip and ease it up slowly along its length.
steps.warn: Don't knock off the small plastic domes over each LED on direct-lit strips; they spread the light.

steps.text: Unscrew the steel back chassis and side brackets if you want the sheet metal. Keep the mains cord and the remote control.
Test each LED strip before you build with it: see Testing below. Keep the bench supply at 30 V or less. Never connect a strip straight to a battery with no resistor or current limit.
steps.warn: LEDs on a supply with no current limit draw too much current and burn out in seconds.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **LED backlight strips.** Aluminium-backed strips of white LEDs wired in series. They make good room and camp lights (see build_led_lighting_12v). A white LED needs roughly 3 V to light, so a strip's voltage depends on how many LEDs it has in series. TV backlight driver chips are built to push strings at up to 120 V and 50 to 400 mA (TI TPS61196), while an iFixit repair guide for an LG set lists a bench supply that gives 12 V and 24 V for testing its strips (iFixit LG 47LN5400). Test each strip before you plan around it.
- **Diffuser and prism sheets.** Thin plastic films that scatter light or steer it forward. One Samsung set also had a Fresnel-type sheet in the stack (iFixit Samsung UE40MU5120). Use them over bare LEDs to soften glare in a lamp or light box. Keep them clean and flat; scratches and fingerprints show.
- **Diffuser plate.** A stiff, milky plastic sheet as big as the screen; Sony lists it separately from the thin diffuser sheet (Sony KDL-32BX330). A large lamp diffuser, or a panel that lets light in where you don't need to see through.
- **Reflector sheet.** The white plastic sheet behind the LEDs; Sony lists main and side reflectors (Sony KDL-32BX330). Line a light box or the inside of a lamp with it to throw more light forward. It is thin plastic: keep it away from flames and hot lamps.
- **Power board.** Turns mains into low-voltage DC: a 5 V standby supply that is always on, plus 12 V, 24 V and other outputs that come on only when the main board sends a power-on signal (iFixit TV boards). The Vizio GV47L board makes 5 V, 12 V and 24 V from 100 to 240 V AC (Vizio GV47L). Running one on its own needs a power-on signal that the main board normally sends, and puts mains on an open board whose big capacitor can hold about 390 V, so leave that to someone who has done it before. Every board switches on differently: read the pin names printed beside its output connector first. One Samsung plug carries standby, power-on, 5 V and 13 V pins (Samsung LN32C350). If you can't work it out, keep it for spare capacitors, heatsinks and coils.
- **Speakers.** Usually two full-range speakers; the Sony KDL-32BX330 has two of 6 W each and the Vizio GV47L two 8 ohm 10 W speakers plus a 20 W woofer (Sony KDL-32BX330; Vizio GV47L). Good for radios, alarms and intercoms with a small amplifier.
- **Main board.** Has the audio amplifier, where the speakers plug in (iFixit TV boards). The infrared remote receiver is often a small separate board (iFixit TV boards lists an IR sensor board; the Samsung LN32C350 has a Function and IR PCB), though on some sets it is screwed to the main board (iFixit LG 42-inch). With the set's remote, the receiver can trigger things at a distance in a project.
- **Steel back chassis, screws, mains cord, and the remote with its batteries.**

## Variations

- **Backlight.** LED sets have strips of LEDs. Older, thicker sets use thin glass CCFL tubes fed by an inverter at about 650 V AC when running (Sony KDL-32BX330). iFixit says some displays from before about 2010 have these mercury-filled tubes (iFixit Device Safety), but Sony's KDL-32BX330 service manual, issued in 2012, still shows CCFL lamps (Sony KDL-32BX330), so treat any set that is not clearly LED as having them. OLED sets make light in each pixel and have no strips, sheets or diffuser plate to salvage.
- **Direct-lit.** Strips run across the whole back, each LED under a small plastic dome, with a white reflector sheet that tucks under the domes and the diffuser and sheets on top (iFixit Samsung UE40MU5120). Strips may be taped down (iFixit LG 55UH6150) or clipped and screwed (iFixit Samsung UE40MU5120).
- **Edge-lit.** Some thin sets have strips along only one or two edges and a clear plastic plate that spreads the light across the screen. The rest of the stack is similar.
- **Layer order.** From the front: LCD panel, thin optical sheets, diffuser plate or clear plate, reflector sheet, LEDs on the steel back. The sheets come out one at a time, and the reflector is held by tabs (iFixit LG 42-inch).
- **Weight.** A 32-inch Sony weighs 5.8 kg without its stand, while an older 47-inch Vizio is about 40 kg (Sony KDL-32BX330; Vizio GV47L). Sony's manual says larger sets need two or more people to carry.
- **Power boards.** Outputs differ by set: 5, 12 and 24 V on the Vizio, 5 V and 13 V pins on the Samsung (Vizio GV47L; Samsung LN32C350). Big boards may boost mains to about 390 V DC inside before stepping it down (TI PMP23488). The backlight driver may be its own board or part of the power board.

## What to leave

- **The LCD panel.** Thin glass with its own timing board and flex strips. It only works with its matching boards, and broken edges cut.
- **CCFL tubes** unless you can lift them out whole. Their mercury escapes when they break.
- **The timing (T-con) board.** It suits only its own panel.
- **The plastic back cover and bezel**, unless you need plastic.

## Testing what you got out

- **LED strips.** With a bench supply, set the current limit low (about 20 mA) and turn the voltage up slowly until the strip glows evenly. Stop at 30 V. A strip that needs more is built for the set's own driver, which can supply up to about 120 V (TI TPS61196): set it aside untested. That voltage is its forward voltage; note it and which end is positive. Then raise the current a little at a time and stop while the strip is still only warm; build_led_lighting_12v suggests about 50 to 100 mA to start. No bench supply: follow the resistor method in build_led_lighting_12v. One dead LED darkens its whole series chain; one repairer found two burnt LEDs on a strip on the dark side of the screen (iFixit LG 55UH6150).
- **Speakers.** Measure across the terminals on the ohms range: a little below the marked impedance (about 6 to 7 ohms for an 8 ohm speaker) means the coil is whole. Open circuit means it is broken.
- **Power board.** Safest tested in the set before teardown: if you have power and the TV still lights up, the board and backlight work. Bench testing a mains board belongs to someone who has done it before.
